title: Pan Am 806
summary: Pan Am Flight 806 departed Auckland on 30 January 1974 with 91 passengers and 10 crew for a flight to Los Angeles with stops at Pago Pago and Honolulu. On approach to Pago Pago, the aircraft encountered microburst wind shear. At 23:40:42, the 707 came into contact with trees 3865 ft short of runway 5 threshold while descending through weather. The aircraft impacted the ground 236 feet further and plowed through dense vegetation for another 539 ft before crashing into a three-foot high rock wall. All four engines were torn from the wings and a post-impact fire consumed most of the aircraft, killing 97 persons. Four crew and passengers initially survived but died later.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the accident was the flightcrew's late recognition and failure to correct in a timely manner an excessive descent rate which developed as a result of the aircraft's penetration through destabilizing wind changes (p. 31). The winds consisted of horizontal and vertical components produced by a heavy rainstorm and influenced by uneven terrain close to the aircraft's approach path. The captain's recognition was hampered by restricted visibility, the illusory effects of a 'blackhole' approach, inadequate monitoring of flight instruments, and the failure of the crew to call out descent rate during the last 15 seconds of flight (p. 31).

factors.evidence: Aircraft encountered microburst-induced wind shear approximately 3 miles from airport creating updraft and headwind causing airspeed gain and glide slope deviation above approach path at 23:40:22.5; wind shear then diminished and aircraft descended at 1,500 fpm for 15 seconds undetected (p. 30-31)

First officer did not switch No. 2 nav receiver from VOR to ILS frequency at final approach fix; glide slope raw data and flight director steering commands displayed only on captain's panel; no descent rate callouts by flight engineer or jumpseat pilot despite exceeding 1,000 fpm maximum for 15 seconds (p. 30-31)

Restricted visibility due to heavy rain shower moving across runway; approach control could not see runway lights from position; VASI lights possibly obscured by rain despite lights being available and operating (p. 7, 30)
Aircraft came into contact with trees 3,865 feet short of runway threshold while descending through destabilizing wind changes; approached at excessive descent rate (p. 8)
Aircraft impacted ground and plowed through dense vegetation before hitting rock wall; aircraft destroyed; 97 fatalities including 4 who initially survived but died later (p. 8)
Aircraft descended at excessive 1,500 fpm rate uncontrolled for 15 seconds due to wind shear effect

events.text: Flight 806 departed Auckland at 20:14 with 91 passengers and 10 crew on board with IFR flight plan to Pago Pago (p. 6-7)

Flight 806 contacted Pago Pago Approach Control 160 miles south of airport; approach control reported weather: ceiling 1,600 ft broken, 4,000 ft broken, 1,000 ft overcast, visibility 1 mile with light rain shower (p. 7)
Pago Pago Approach Control cleared flight to VORTAC (p. 7)
Flight left FL-200 and began approach descent at 23:24:40 (p. 7)
Approach control cleared flight for ILS DME runway 5 approach via 20-mile arc south-southwest; reported to leave 5,000 feet (p. 7)
Flight requested direction and velocity of Pago Pago winds; told 360° variable from 020° at 10-45 knots (p. 7)
Flight reported out of 5,500 feet and intercepted 226° radial of Pago Pago VOR; approach control confirmed inbound on localizer, winds 010° at 15 gusting 20 knots (p. 7)
Approach control reported power failure at airport; first officer confirmed still receiving VOR, ILS and lights (p. 7)

Approach control asked about runway lights visibility; flight confirmed seeing them. Approach control reported bad rain shower. At 23:39:29 first officer reported at 5 DME with lights still appearing bright (p. 7)
First officer stated "You're a little high"; four seconds later sound of electric stabilizer trim actuation heard on CVR indicating aircraft above glide slope during microburst encounter (p. 7)
Radio altimeter warning tone sounded twice; at 23:40:33.5 first officer called "You're at minimums" indicating descent through minimum altitude (p. 7-8)

First officer reported "Field in sight" then "Turn to your right" followed by "hundred and forty knots" - last CVR communication; aircraft descending at 1,500 fpm with inadequate monitoring of instruments (p. 8)

Aircraft struck trees at 113 ft elevation and 3,865 ft short of runway threshold; impacted ground 236 ft farther; continued through jungle vegetation striking 3-foot-high lava rock wall stopping 3,090 ft from runway threshold; all four engines torn from wings (p. 8)

Aircraft destroyed by impact and subsequent fire; 97 fatalities (86 passengers, 10 crew, 1 house resident); 4 crew and passengers initially survived but died later; fire and rescue response delayed by rain, barriers, and terrain (p. 8)

notes: Read History of Flight section (pages 6-8), Conclusions section (pages 30-31), Probable Cause section (page 31)
Extracted 13 detailed events with specific clock times from CVR and approach control communications
Probable cause: late recognition and failure to correct excessive descent rate resulting from aircraft penetration through microburst wind shear (p. 31)
Contributing factors: restricted visibility, blackhole approach illusion, inadequate instrument monitoring, no descent rate callouts (p. 30-31)
Recommendations include CFR amendments regarding pilot recent experience requirements, VASI/PAPI standardization, and wind shear training (p. 31+)
